about: Authored query pairs on Pagila for tools/sample_db_bench.py. label: 'equivalent' or 'different' under the declared keys minus 'drop' (not_null:T.c, pk:T, fk:T.c). A 'different' pair carries a witness: 'real' (the two queries already differ on the Pagila data) or a small database (missing columns are completed with legal values) that satisfies the remaining declarations and separates them. 'sibling' names the pair it negates. Pagila's payment table declares no foreign key and the composite key (payment_date, payment_id), as upstream does for the table as a whole, so the payment pairs are different under the declarations even where the data happens to agree.

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: rental.inventory_id is NOT NULL and references inventory's key: every rental joins exactly one inventory row
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id, r.rental_date FROM rental AS r JOIN inventory AS i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
pairs.right: SELECT rental_id, rental_date FROM rental

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: film.original_language_id may be NULL (it is NULL in every film of the data): such a film joins no language
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id, f.title FROM film AS f JOIN language AS l ON f.original_language_id = l.language_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key a rental may name an inventory row that does not exist
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id, r.rental_date FROM rental AS r JOIN inventory AS i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
pairs.right: SELECT rental_id, rental_date FROM rental

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without inventory's key two inventory rows may share an id, and the join repeats the rental
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id, r.rental_date FROM rental AS r JOIN inventory AS i ON r.inventory_id = i.inventory_id
pairs.right: SELECT rental_id, rental_date FROM rental

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: rental.customer_id and customer.address_id are NOT NULL foreign keys to keys: both joins keep every rental exactly once
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id FROM rental AS r JOIN customer AS c ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN address AS a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
pairs.right: SELECT rental_id FROM rental

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key customer.address_id a customer may have an address that does not exist
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id FROM rental AS r JOIN customer AS c ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id JOIN address AS a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
pairs.right: SELECT rental_id FROM rental

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film.original_language_id references language's key: a non-NULL value always finds exactly one language, a NULL finds none
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id FROM film AS f JOIN language AS l ON f.original_language_id = l.language_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE original_language_id IS NOT NULL

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the foreign key a film may name an original language that does not exist
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id FROM film AS f JOIN language AS l ON f.original_language_id = l.language_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE original_language_id IS NOT NULL

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: address_id is address's key: the LEFT JOIN neither drops nor repeats a customer
pairs.left: SELECT c.customer_id, c.last_name FROM customer AS c LEFT JOIN address AS a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id, last_name FROM customer

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: inventory.film_id is not unique: a film with several copies is repeated by the LEFT JOIN
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id, f.title FROM film AS f LEFT JOIN inventory AS i ON i.film_id = f.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without address's key two addresses may share an id, and the LEFT JOIN repeats the customer
pairs.left: SELECT c.customer_id, c.last_name FROM customer AS c LEFT JOIN address AS a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id, last_name FROM customer

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film_actor.actor_id is a NOT NULL foreign key to actor's key
pairs.left: SELECT fa.film_id, fa.last_update FROM film_actor AS fa JOIN actor AS a ON fa.actor_id = a.actor_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, last_update FROM film_actor

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film_embedding.film_id is the table's key and a NOT NULL foreign key to film: every embedding joins exactly one film
pairs.left: SELECT e.film_id, e.embedding FROM film_embedding AS e JOIN film AS f ON e.film_id = f.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, embedding FROM film_embedding

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: nothing requires a film to have an embedding: a film without one is dropped by the join (every film of the data has one)
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id, f.title FROM film AS f JOIN film_embedding AS e ON e.film_id = f.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: payment declares no foreign key: upstream declares payment's customer, rental and staff keys on the first six of its 55 partitions only, so the table as a whole guarantees nothing (every payment of the data does have a customer)
pairs.left: SELECT p.payment_id, p.amount FROM payment AS p JOIN customer AS c ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id
pairs.right: SELECT payment_id, amount FROM payment

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film_id is film's key: joining a film to itself on it keeps every film once
pairs.left: SELECT a.film_id, a.title FROM film AS a JOIN film AS b ON a.film_id = b.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without film's key two films may share an id, and the self join repeats them
pairs.left: SELECT a.film_id, a.title FROM film AS a JOIN film AS b ON a.film_id = b.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film_id is film's key and is selected
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT film_id, title FROM film
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without film's key two identical film rows may exist
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT film_id, title FROM film
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, title FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: rating is not a key: many films share one
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT rating FROM film
pairs.right: SELECT rating FROM film

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: (actor_id, film_id) is film_actor's key and both are selected
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT actor_id, film_id FROM film_actor
pairs.right: SELECT actor_id, film_id FROM film_actor

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: film_id alone is only part of the key: a film has several actors
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT film_id FROM film_actor
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film_actor

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: the join is to address's key, so no customer is repeated, and customer_id is customer's key
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id, c.last_name FROM customer AS c JOIN address AS a ON c.address_id = a.address_id
pairs.right: SELECT c.customer_id, c.last_name FROM customer AS c JOIN address AS a ON c.address_id = a.address_id

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: rental.customer_id is not unique: the join repeats a customer once per rental
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id FROM customer AS c JOIN rental AS r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id
pairs.right: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customer AS c JOIN rental AS r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: (payment_date, payment_id) is payment's declared key and both are selected
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT payment_date, payment_id, amount FROM payment
pairs.right: SELECT payment_date, payment_id, amount FROM payment

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: payment_id alone is not a declared key (the key is (payment_date, payment_id)): two payments may share an id and an amount; no payment of the data does
pairs.left: SELECT DISTINCT payment_id, amount FROM payment
pairs.right: SELECT payment_id, amount FROM payment
pairs.known_prover_bug: bounded checker: a DATETIME model value is clamped to 0001-01-01 on extraction (bounded_equivalence._model_value), so two payments with different payment_date come out with the same composite key and the counterexample violates it

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: rental.rental_date is NOT NULL, so COUNT(rental_date) counts every row
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(rental_date) FROM rental
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rental

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: rental.return_date is NULL for rentals still out
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(return_date) FROM rental
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rental

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: store_id depends on customer_id, customer's key
pairs.left: SELECT c.customer_id, c.last_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM customer AS c JOIN rental AS r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.last_name, c.store_id
pairs.right: SELECT c.customer_id, c.last_name, COUNT(*) AS n FROM customer AS c JOIN rental AS r ON r.customer_id = c.customer_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.last_name

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a customer's rentals are handled by several staff members, so grouping by staff_id too splits the count
pairs.left: SELECT r.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM rental AS r GROUP BY r.customer_id, r.staff_id
pairs.right: SELECT r.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM rental AS r GROUP BY r.customer_id

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: customer_id is customer's key
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM customer
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customer

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a customer has many rentals
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM rental
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM rental

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: payment_id alone is not a declared key: two payments may share an id (none do in the data)
pairs.left: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT payment_id) FROM payment
pairs.right: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM payment
pairs.known_prover_bug: bounded checker: a DATETIME model value is clamped to 0001-01-01 on extraction (bounded_equivalence._model_value), so two payments with different payment_date come out with the same composite key and the counterexample violates it

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a condition on the group key can filter before grouping
pairs.left: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) AS n FROM film GROUP BY rating HAVING rating <> 'G'
pairs.right: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) AS n FROM film WHERE rating <> 'G' GROUP BY rating

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a group with no matching row disappears from the first query and counts 0 in the second
pairs.left: SELECT rating, COUNT(*) AS n FROM film WHERE length > 100 GROUP BY rating
pairs.right: SELECT rating, COUNTIF(length > 100) AS n FROM film GROUP BY rating

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a filter on the grouping column commutes with GROUP BY
pairs.left: SELECT * FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM rental GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE customer_id = 1
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n FROM rental WHERE customer_id = 1 GROUP BY customer_id

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film_id is film's key: grouping the LEFT JOIN by it counts each film's copies once, as the correlated subquery does
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id, COUNT(i.inventory_id) AS copies FROM film AS f LEFT JOIN inventory AS i ON i.film_id = f.film_id GROUP BY f.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT f.film_id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.film_id = f.film_id) AS copies FROM film AS f

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without film's key two films may share an id: grouping merges them, the subquery does not
pairs.left: SELECT f.film_id, COUNT(i.inventory_id) AS copies FROM film AS f LEFT JOIN inventory AS i ON i.film_id = f.film_id GROUP BY f.film_id
pairs.right: SELECT f.film_id, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.film_id = f.film_id) AS copies FROM film AS f

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: IN and a correlated EXISTS agree
pairs.left: SELECT customer_id FROM customer WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM payment WHERE amount > 10)
pairs.right: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customer AS c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM payment AS p WHERE p.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p.amount > 10)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a customer with several payments over 5 is repeated by the join
pairs.left: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customer AS c JOIN payment AS p ON p.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE p.amount > 5
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id FROM customer WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM payment WHERE amount > 5)

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film_id is film's key: the join cannot repeat an inventory row
pairs.left: SELECT i.inventory_id FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.film_id IN (SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE rating = 'R')
pairs.right: SELECT i.inventory_id FROM inventory AS i JOIN film AS f ON f.film_id = i.film_id WHERE f.rating = 'R'

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without film's key two films may share an id, and the join repeats the inventory row
pairs.left: SELECT i.inventory_id FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.film_id IN (SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE rating = 'R')
pairs.right: SELECT i.inventory_id FROM inventory AS i JOIN film AS f ON f.film_id = i.film_id WHERE f.rating = 'R'

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: inventory.film_id is NOT NULL, so NOT IN and NOT EXISTS agree
pairs.left: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE film_id NOT IN (SELECT film_id FROM inventory)
pairs.right: SELECT f.film_id FROM film AS f WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.film_id = f.film_id)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: film.original_language_id is NULL in every film, so NOT IN returns no row while NOT EXISTS returns every language
pairs.left: SELECT language_id FROM language WHERE language_id NOT IN (SELECT original_language_id FROM film)
pairs.right: SELECT l.language_id FROM language AS l WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM film AS f WHERE f.original_language_id = l.language_id)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: without the NOT NULL a NULL film_id in inventory makes NOT IN return no row
pairs.left: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE film_id NOT IN (SELECT film_id FROM inventory)
pairs.right: SELECT f.film_id FROM film AS f WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM inventory AS i WHERE i.film_id = f.film_id)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: UNION ALL keeps the duplicates UNION DISTINCT removes
pairs.left: SELECT customer_id FROM rental UNION ALL SELECT customer_id FROM payment
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id FROM rental UNION DISTINCT SELECT customer_id FROM payment

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film.rental_duration is NOT NULL, so every film satisfies exactly one of the two filters
pairs.left: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE rental_duration > 4 UNION ALL SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE rental_duration <= 4
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: film.length may be NULL: such a film satisfies neither filter (no film of the data has a NULL length)
pairs.left: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE length > 100 UNION ALL SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE length <= 100
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: rental.customer_id and payment.customer_id are NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT customer_id FROM rental INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT customer_id FROM payment
pairs.right: SELECT DISTINCT r.customer_id FROM rental AS r WHERE r.customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM payment)

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: INTERSECT matches NULLs, IN does not: a NULL email in both tables is returned by the first query only
pairs.left: SELECT email FROM customer INTERSECT DISTINCT SELECT email FROM staff
pairs.right: SELECT DISTINCT c.email FROM customer AS c WHERE c.email IN (SELECT email FROM staff)

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: the WHERE condition rejects the NULL-padded rows of the LEFT JOIN
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id, p.amount FROM rental AS r LEFT JOIN payment AS p ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id WHERE p.amount > 5
pairs.right: SELECT r.rental_id, p.amount FROM rental AS r JOIN payment AS p ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id WHERE p.amount > 5

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: the condition accepts NULL: rentals without a payment survive the LEFT JOIN only
pairs.left: SELECT r.rental_id, p.amount FROM rental AS r LEFT JOIN payment AS p ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id WHERE p.amount > 5 OR p.amount IS NULL
pairs.right: SELECT r.rental_id, p.amount FROM rental AS r JOIN payment AS p ON p.rental_id = r.rental_id WHERE p.amount > 5 OR p.amount IS NULL

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: customer.address_id is NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT customer_id FROM customer WHERE address_id IS NULL
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id FROM customer WHERE FALSE

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: customer.email may be NULL (no customer of the data has a NULL email)
pairs.left: SELECT customer_id FROM customer WHERE email IS NULL
pairs.right: SELECT customer_id FROM customer WHERE FALSE

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: actor.first_name is NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT actor_id, COALESCE(first_name, 'x') AS first_name FROM actor
pairs.right: SELECT actor_id, first_name FROM actor

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: address.address2 is NULL for some addresses
pairs.left: SELECT address_id, COALESCE(address2, 'x') AS address2 FROM address
pairs.right: SELECT address_id, address2 FROM address

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: film.rental_duration is NOT NULL
pairs.left: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE NOT (rental_duration = 3)
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE rental_duration <> 3

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: film.length may be NULL: NOT (NULL = 100) is NULL, so the film is dropped by the first query and kept by the second (no film of the data has a NULL length)
pairs.left: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE NOT (length = 100)
pairs.right: SELECT film_id FROM film WHERE length <> 100 OR length IS NULL

pairs.label: equivalent
pairs.why: a filter on the PARTITION BY column commutes with the window
pairs.left: SELECT film_id, rating, r FROM (SELECT film_id, rating, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length) AS r FROM film) WHERE rating = 'PG'
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, rating, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length) AS r FROM film WHERE rating = 'PG'

pairs.label: different
pairs.why: a filter on another column changes the ranks
pairs.left: SELECT film_id, rating, r FROM (SELECT film_id, rating, length, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length) AS r FROM film) WHERE length > 100
pairs.right: SELECT film_id, rating, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY rating ORDER BY length) AS r FROM film WHERE length > 100
